Following a gestation period of 40 days [tg = 40 days], timed during the summer months when maternal body temperatures stabilize near 39 °C [T = 39 °C], females give birth to litters averaging four pups [N_R_i = litters averaging four pups]. This reproductive output is produced about 1.8 times per year [F_R_i = about 1.8 times per year], yielding a substantial annual recruitment potential for a small sciurid. The neonatal mass is remarkably low relative to the mother's own adult size, necessitating an intense period of maternal investment through lactation. The dependency of these altricial young on maternal milk is absolute during the initial weeks postpartum, with the pups exhibiting minimal thermoregulatory ability and relying entirely on the mother for warmth and nutrition. Such a pronounced altricial strategy is typical of tree squirrels, allowing the mother to conserve energetic resources during gestation while shifting the bulk of investment to the post-natal period.

Weaning, defined as the cessation of milk intake and the onset of nutritional independence, occurs at 58 days after birth [tx = 58 days after birth] under the same thermoneutral conditions of 39 °C [T = 39 °C] that characterize the maternal nest environment. At this developmental milestone, the young have achieved a wet body mass of 46.2 grams [Wwx = 46.2 grams], representing a more than thirteenfold increase from their birth weight. This rapid mass gain is fueled by the high-fat content of flying squirrel milk, which supports accelerated growth rates necessary for the young to reach independence before the onset of winter. The 58-day period marks a critical transition, as the juveniles begin to consume solid foods such as mast, fungi, and insects while gradually reducing their reliance on the mother. Post-weaning survival is strongly dependent on the availability of cached food resources, particularly in northern portions of the species' range where autumn is brief. The weaning mass of 46.2 grams is a useful predictor of juvenile condition and subsequent overwinter survival in wild populations.

Sexual maturation in Glaucomys volans is a gradual process that culminates in reproductive capability at 210 days after birth [tp = 210 days after birth], timed to coincide with the late winter breeding season when ambient temperatures remain low but maternal body temperatures are maintained at 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This relatively long juvenile period reflects the time required to achieve the ultimate adult body mass of 65.4 grams [Wwi = 65.4 grams], a size at which individuals can effectively compete for nesting cavities and food resources. The 210-day interval from birth to puberty is notably protracted for a rodent of this body size, likely shaped by the seasonal constraints of the deciduous forests they inhabit. Juveniles born early in the spring breeding season have a distinct advantage, reaching sexual maturity in time for the following year's reproductive window. In contrast, late-born individuals may delay their first breeding until their second year, a flexibility that buffers population dynamics against annual fluctuations in food abundance. The attainment of 65.4 grams appears to be a threshold above which reproductive hormones become fully activated.

The maximum reproductive rate achievable under optimal conditions at 39 °C [T = 39 °C] is defined by the combination of four pups per litter [N_R_i = four pups per litter] and 1.8 litters per year [F_R_i = 1.8 litters per year], with the latter dictated by the length of the breeding season and the time required to rear each litter to independence. Field studies have documented females producing a second litter immediately after weaning the first, with the weaning period of 58 days after birth [tx = 58 days after birth] setting a minimum inter-litter interval at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This schedule is only possible when ambient temperatures allow the mother to maintain a stable core temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C] without excessive thermoregulatory costs. In particularly mast-rich years, some females may even attempt a third litter, though such events are comparatively rare and often result in reduced overwinter survival for the mother. The reproductive biology of this species thus represents a finely tuned balance between current reproductive effort and future survival, constrained by both temperature-dependent metabolic rates and seasonal food availability. Litter sizes larger than four are occasionally observed but typically result in reduced weaning masses.

Longevity records for this species indicate a maximum lifespan of 19 years [am = 19 years] under captive conditions where predators are absent and food is consistently available, though wild individuals rarely exceed half that duration at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This lifespan, achieved under thermoneutral conditions of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], is remarkable for a mammal of such small body size, as the ultimate adult wet weight of 65.4 grams [Wwi = 65.4 grams] would ordinarily predict a much shorter life expectancy. The disparity between predicted and observed longevity likely reflects the species' use of torpor during cold periods, a metabolic strategy that conserves energy and reduces oxidative damage. In the wild, predation by owls, snakes, and arboreal mammals imposes a heavy mortality toll, such that the average lifespan is closer to two to three years. Nonetheless, the physiological capacity for extended survival is evident in captive populations, where individuals have been known to reproduce well into their fifth year. This extended reproductive window allows females to offset occasional years of breeding failure, contributing to the species' demographic resilience across its broad geographic range.
